city_history.founded: 1325 (as Mexica/Aztec capital Tenochtitlan; the symbolic date 13 March 1325 was fixed in 1925 for the 600th anniversary). Modern Mexico City was re-founded by the Spanish in 1521 on the ruins of Tenochtitlan.
city_history.significance: Capital of Mexico and the oldest capital city in the Americas. Built on an island in former Lake Texcoco, Tenochtitlan was the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas and the hub of the Aztec Empire until its fall to Hernán Cortés and Tlaxcaltec allies in 1521. Today one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world and Mexico's political, cultural and economic center. Estadio Azteca/Banorte sits at ~2,200 m (7,220 ft) elevation in the Tlalpan/Coyoacán area.
city_history.football_culture: Mexico City is the beating heart of Mexican football. Estadio Azteca/Banorte is home to Club América — the country's most successful and most polarizing club — and the regular home of El Tri, whose qualifiers and big internationals fill the bowl. The capital hosts the Clásico Capitalino (América vs Cruz Azul / Pumas) and the stadium staged two of football's most mythologized moments: Pelé's 1970 coronation and Maradona's 1986 double against England. Altitude (~2,200 m) and a partisan home crowd make it one of the most intimidating venues in world football.

stadium_history_facts: Opened 29 May 1966; inaugural match Club América vs Torino (2–2). VERIFIED.
Designed by Mexican architects Pedro Ramírez Vázquez and Rafael Mijares Alcérreca. VERIFIED.

Owned by Grupo Televisa since 1966; operations spun off into the publicly-listed Grupo Ollamani (created 31 Jan 2024), which now OPERATES the stadium and controls Club América. Ultimate ownership remains within the Televisa/Azcárraga group. (CORRECTED: original sheet wrongly stated Ollamani 'owns/operates'.)
Permanent home of Club América since 1966 and the regular home of the Mexico national team.
First stadium to host two World Cup finals (1970 and 1986) and the only stadium to host three men's World Cups (1970, 1986, 2026); first to host three World Cup opening matches.
Hosted the 1970 final (Brazil 4–1 Italy) and the 1986 final (Argentina 3–2 West Germany), plus Maradona's 'Hand of God' / 'Goal of the Century' quarter-final vs England in 1986.
Also a major non-football venue: hosted events of the 1968 Summer Olympics, the 1975 Pan-American Games, and the 1999 FIFA Confederations Cup.
Sits at ~2,200 m (7,220 ft) elevation — a notable altitude factor for visiting teams.

On 14 March 2025 Grupo Financiero Banorte acquired naming rights and the venue was renamed Estadio Banorte; for the 2026 World Cup FIFA uses the neutral name 'Mexico City Stadium' (Estadio Ciudad de México) because corporate names are barred during the tournament. VERIFIED.
Closed for its most extensive renovation from May 2024; reopened 28 March 2026 with a Mexico vs Portugal friendly (0–0). VERIFIED.
